Abstract
Objective: Widespread structural pathology in the limbic system is a hallmark of 
temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). In this work, we sought to describe a comprehen­
sive readout of limbic abnormalities in TLE using neurite orientation distribution 
and density imaging (NODDI).
Methods: This is a retrospective study of patients with drug-­resistant TLE and 
healthy controls who underwent research magnetic resonance imaging. We es­
timated the degree of deviation of the NODDI parameters neurite density index 
(NDI) and orientation dispersion index (ODI) from healthy controls in limbic 
regions in the form of univariate z-­scores. We calculated a multivariate deviation 
score combining both NDI and ODI (Mahalanobis distance). A summary score 
representing the overall level of deviation across limbic regions was then com­
puted using the sum of regional deviation scores. We next assessed the diagnostic 
performance of summary scores in lateralizing TLE as well as associations with 
neuropsychological deficits and 12-­month surgical outcome.
Results: The Mahalanobis distance revealed unique patterns of abnormalities 
between TLE participants (n = 74) and controls (n = 42), with only four of 18 
(22%) areas displaying overlapping univariate and multivariate deviations. The 
multivariate summary score achieved the highest diagnostic accuracy in clinical 
lateralization of nonlesional TLE (area under the curve [AUC] = .95, 95% confi­
dence interval [CI] = .77–1). Among surgical patients (n = 30), summary scores 
corresponding to the hemisphere ipsilateral and contralateral to surgery were 
predictive of seizure freedom at 12 months (AUC = .84, 95% CI = .76–.93).
Significance: We demonstrate unique patterns of abnormalities in neurite den­
sity and coherence in limbic microstructure in TLE. A summary score accounting 
for deviations in both neurite density and coherence achieved high diagnos­
tic accuracy in clinical lateralization of TLE and was associated with surgical

1  |  INTRODUCTION
Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is the most well character­
ized of the epilepsies. It is a diverse syndrome that can 
be further subcategorized based on presumed location of 
seizure onset. These syndromes include mesial TLE, ne­
ocortical TLE, bilateral TLE, and extratemporal epilep­
sies with seizure spread to the temporal lobe, so-­called 
temporal-­plus epilepsy.1 The neurobiological phenom­
enon shared by these distinct clinical entities is their 
propensity for seizures to develop or propagate within 
limbic circuits. Although the hippocampus has been the 
most intensely scrutinized structure in the limbic net­
work for its role in seizure generation and propagation, 
both animal and human data point to more widespread 
anatomic and electrophysiologic disturbances in the 
limbic system. In post-­status epilepticus animal models, 
which are thought to share the most characteristics with 
human mesial TLE,2 neuronal loss and gliosis occur in 
multiple regions of the limbic system, including dam­
age in amygdala, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, 
and entorhinal and piriform cortices.3 Similar neuro­
pathologic findings are seen in human TLE, with wide­
spread changes in hippocampus, amygdala, entorhinal 
cortex, and piriform cortex.4,5 Furthermore, temporal 
lobe white matter is understudied but also implicated in 
the pathogenesis of TLE.6
Large-­scale magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) stud­
ies have recapitulated these findings in  vivo, showing 
widespread structural abnormalities in both gray and 
white matter across all forms of epilepsy. In TLE, these 
structural abnormalities are most pronounced in the 
temporal lobe ipsilateral to seizure onset and include 
both gray matter (i.e., hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, 
parahippocampal gyrus, temporal pole)7 and white mat­
ter regions (i.e., cingulum, fornix, uncinate fasciculus).8 
These studies are informative in that they provide in­
formation about the localization of structural changes 
in TLE at the group level (i.e., in the average patient); 
however, even in well-­characterized clinical syndromes, 
individual patients have a heterogeneous profile of struc­
tural abnormalities across brain regions.9,10 We currently 
lack methods to (1) comprehensively profile the burden 
of damage across multiple brain regions, such as those 
in the limbic system; and (2) characterize individual 
patient-­level patterns of structural abnormalities across 
multiple brain regions. These tools could be used to gen­
erate a single variable readout of the burden of damage 
across a range of relevant structures (i.e., the limbic sys­
tem). This could then be evaluated as a diagnostic and 
prognostic biomarker in focal epilepsy.
There is also the well-­recognized phenomenon of non­
lesional TLE, where there is no MRI-­visible epileptogenic 
structural lesion. These patients tend to have worse sur­
gical outcomes, presumably because epileptogenic net­
works are harder to identify. Advanced diffusion MRI 
(dMRI) techniques such as neurite orientation distribu­
tion and density imaging (NODDI) have the potential 
to map microstructural abnormalities of dendrites and 
axons (i.e., neurites) in vivo,11 which may be undetectable 
with other techniques. Whereas diffusion tensor imaging 
models water diffusion in a single compartment, NODDI 
adopts a tissue model that distinguishes water diffusion 
in intracellular, extracellular, and cerebrospinal fluid 
(CSF) compartments. This enables voxelwise estimates of 
outcomes, warranting further study as a putative biomarker in TLE to be used 
alongside clinical data.

Key points
• A multivariate measure for mapping deviations 
in brain microstructure was developed to char­
acterize limbic pathology in patients with tem­
poral lobe epilepsy.
• The multivariate summary score represents 
the distance of the NODDI parameters neurite 
density index and orientation dispersion index 
from healthy controls.
• The multivariate summary score achieved high 
diagnostic accuracy in clinical lateralization of 
both lesional and nonlesional temporal lobe 
epilepsy.
• Temporal lobe epilepsy patients with right-­
lateralized neuropsychological deficits had higher 
multivariate scores in the right hemisphere.
• Summary scores corresponding to the hemi­
sphere ipsilateral and contralateral to surgery 
were predictive of seizure freedom at 12 months.

neurite density index (NDI), the packing density of neu­
rites; orientation dispersion index (ODI), a measure of 
the coherence of neurites; and free water fraction (FWF), 
which estimates the amount of partial volume effects from 
CSF contamination.11 Prior studies have used NODDI to 
demonstrate microstructural abnormalities in TLE; how­
ever, most studies have either focused on a single parame­
ter (e.g., NDI)12,13 or a single region (e.g., hippocampus),14 
or not taken advantage of the opportunity to correct for 
partial volume effects (e.g., by using the FWF),15,16 which 
bias estimates of NDI and ODI and are particularly prob­
lematic for structures abutting CSF spaces such as the 
hippocampus.
In this work, we sought to overcome the above limita­
tions by characterizing microstructural abnormalities in 
the limbic network in TLE using multivariate methods 
that account for the unique information from NDI and 
ODI. We also leveraged the FWF map to perform cor­
rection for partial volume effects of CSF to produce less 
biased estimates of NDI and ODI. We first investigated 
the pattern of abnormalities at individual regions in the 
limbic network. The extent of “abnormality” is defined 
via normative modeling, a tool that holds promise for pre­
cision medicine in epilepsy,17 where regional deviations 
are defined by the distance from a healthy control cohort 
using age and gender as covariates. We aim to describe a 
more comprehensive readout of abnormalities in the lim­
bic network by examining multiple gray matter structures, 
including piriform cortex, an understudied but highly ep­
ileptogenic structure, as well as temporal lobe white mat­
ter tracts, which are also implicated in the pathogenesis 
of TLE but much less studied. We first investigated the 
pattern of deviations at individual regions in the limbic 
network and then aggregated these measures into a single 
summary measure of overall burden of limbic microstruc­
tural abnormality. To validate this summary measure, we 
assessed its diagnostic performance in clinical lateraliza­
tion of TLE. We show that multivariate measures of limbic 
microstructural abnormalities, accounting for the unique 
effects of NDI and ODI, display high diagnostic accuracy 
in clinical lateralization of TLE and associate with neuro­
psychological deficits and surgical outcomes.
2  |  MATERIALS AND METHODS
2.1  |  Study participants
This study is a retrospective analysis of patients with 
drug-­resistant TLE who underwent a research 3-­T MRI 
including structural and diffusion-­weighted imag­
ing during presurgical evaluation at the Hospital of the 
University of Pennsylvania. Diagnosis of TLE was based 
on multidisciplinary review in the Penn Epilepsy Surgical 
Conference of each patient's habitual seizure semiology, 
video-­electroencephalographic (video-­EEG) evaluation, 
structural MRI, fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission 
tomography (FDG-­PET), neuropsychological testing, and 
intracranial EEG, when indicated. We also included a co­
hort of healthy controls who underwent a research 3-­T 
MRI at the same institution.
2.2  |  Standard protocol approvals, 
registrations, and patient consents
The study protocol was approved by the institutional re­
view board of the University of Pennsylvania, and all par­
ticipants provided informed consent.
2.3  |  Image acquisition
Brain MRIs were performed on two separate 3-­T scanners 
(Siemens Magnetom TrioTim and Siemens Magnetom 
Prisma Fit). Structural imaging used in this study in­
cluded a three-­dimensional T1-­weighted image and whole 
brain dMRI with an echo planar sequence. Details of each 
image acquisition protocol are provided in Table S1.
2.4  |  Image processing
Structural and dMRI data were visually inspected for arti­
facts both before and after preprocessing. MRI data were 
preprocessed using QSIPrep 0.12.2,18 which performed 
anatomical and diffusion data preprocessing. Briefly, ana­
tomical data preprocessing included correction for inten­
sity nonuniformity, brain extraction, and registration to 
standard space. Diffusion data preprocessing included de­
noising, B1 field inhomogeneity correction, head motion 
and eddy current correction, susceptibility distortion cor­
rection using either field maps or reverse phase-­encoded 
images (see Table S1), and resampling to anatomical space. 
The NODDI model was fitted to preprocessed dMRI data 
using the NODDI toolbox.11 To reduce bias from CSF par­
tial volume effects, we utilized the method described by 
Parker et al.15 to create tissue-­weighted maps of NDI and 
ODI. Using the deformable SyN registration algorithm 
from Advanced Normalization Tools (ANTs),19 each par­
ticipant's preprocessed structural MRI was registered to 
the JHU-­MNI-­ss (Eve) template20 followed by interpola­
tion of atlas labels into structural space. For analysis of the 
piriform cortex, we utilized piriform cortex atlases from 
a dataset of 30 healthy controls as described in Steinbart 
et al.21 Piriform cortex labels were then resampled into the

2.5  |  Region of interest analysis
Mean values of NDI and ODI were extracted from

lum, column/body and cres stria terminalis of fornix, 
uncinate fasciculus] from the Eve atlas as well as the 
piriform cortex). To mitigate confounds introduced by 
use of different MRI protocols, scalar means for each 
ROI were harmonized using ComBat, a validated batch

cluded in the model were age, gender, and group (i.e., 
control vs. TLE). ROIs with scalar values greater than 
three scaled median absolute deviations from the me­
dian were considered artifactual and removed prior to 
analysis. As in our prior work,24,25 for each ROI, we re­
gressed out age and gender from the scalar means using 
robust linear regression models to mitigate the effects 
of outliers. Models were fitted using only observations 
from controls with age and gender as independent vari­
ables and the mean of the respective NODDI variable 
(e.g., NDI) as the dependent variable. Age and gender 
were then regressed out for both patients and controls 
using the residuals from the above regression. We then 
converted the residuals to z-­scores using the mean and 
SD of the control cohort. This amounts to an ROI-­level 
summary statistic, one each for NDI and ODI, for each 
participant after accounting for the effects of age and 
gender.10 To minimize bias when calculating z-­scores 
for controls, we excluded that participant's data from 
the calculation of mean and SD of the control cohort.
2.6  |  Multivariate analysis
We also used the residuals across both NDI and ODI for 
each mesial temporal ROI to calculate the Mahalanobis 
(M)-­distance, a multivariate generalization of the z-­
score.25,26 This results in a single ROI-­level summary 
statistic taking into account the unique contributions of 
NDI and ODI to cerebral microstructure after accounting 
for age and gender. Similar to calculation of z-­scores for 
controls, we excluded the participant's data from the refer­
ence cohort when calculating distance to minimize bias. 
An example of this pipeline is shown for one exemplar re­
gion in Figure 1.

To assess for left–right asymmetries in univariate z-­scores 
and M-­distance, we calculated the laterality index (LI)

2.8  |  Statistical analysis
Assumptions of normality were assessed both visually and 
via the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. As most variables were 
not normally distributed, we utilized the nonparametric 
Mann–Whitney U-­test for comparisons involving two groups 
and the Kruskal–Wallis test for comparisons involving three 
or more groups. Chi-­squared or Fisher exact test were used 
for categorical data where appropriate. When performing 
statistical tests for individual ROIs, we performed multiple 
comparisons correction using the Benjamini and Hochberg 
procedure.27 All analyses were carried out using MATLAB 
2023b (Natick, Massachusetts: The MathWorks Inc.; 2023).
2.8.1  |  Diagnostic performance of LI in 
clinical lateralization of TLE
Using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, we 
assessed the diagnostic accuracy of the LI of ROI-­level 
NDI and ODI z-­scores and M-­distance measures against 
the laterality of TLE (i.e., right vs. left) determined at 
multidisciplinary conference. We also assessed the diag­
nostic accuracy of the sum of regionwise LIs separately 
for z-­scores and M-­distance of NDI/ODI. To account for 
the impact of visible MRI lesions on NDI and ODI, we 
also constructed ROC curves for MRI nonlesional pa­
tients only. These analyses were primarily undertaken to 
validate the summary measures against the known clini­
cal lateralization, but it is worth noting that even after 
extensive noninvasive testing (e.g., scalp video-­EEG, 
MRI, FDG-­PET), a patient's epilepsy may not be well lat­
eralized, and thus additional measures of laterality such 
as those derived from NODDI may be informative.
2.8.2  |  Burden of limbic microstructural 
abnormalities and associations with 
neuropsychological deficits and surgical outcome
To evaluate associations with neuropsychological deficits 
and surgical outcome, we calculated the sum of the M-­
distance for the nine mesial temporal ROIs in each hemi­
sphere and labeled these as ipsilateral or contralateral 
according to the clinical lateralization of each participant. 
This summary score is a single measurement of multivari­
ate deviation in each hemisphere for which we evaluated 
associations with neuropsychological deficits and surgi­
cal outcome. To increase statistical power in our analy­
sis of surgical outcome, right TLE participants' data were 
flipped so that all unilateral TLE patients were considered 
to have left hemispheric lateralization. We investigated the

selected the model with the highest accuracy for testing

3  |  RESULTS
3.1  |  Demographic and clinical 
information
We enrolled 85 participants with TLE and 50 healthy con­
trols. Fourteen participants (seven patients and seven con­
trols) were excluded due to low MRI quality or artifact. An 
additional four patients with prior temporal lobe surgery and 
one control with a brain lesion were excluded. Demographic 
and clinical information for the analytic cohort (TLE = 74 
and healthy control = 42) is presented in Table 1. Among 
participants with TLE, 35% were considered nonlesional by 
MRI. Most patients had unilateral TLE (36% right and 50% 
left), with 10 having bilateral TLE (13%) based on noninva­
sive evaluation. Among those with unilateral TLE (n = 64), 
73% were judged to have well-­lateralized TLE based on 
noninvasive data. Twenty-­five (34%) patients underwent 
intracranial EEG. Thirty-­four (46%) underwent ablative or 
resective surgery, for which 1-­year outcomes were available 
in 32 (43%). Two such surgeries were judged to be palliative.
3.2  |  TLE distance from controls
The distribution of regional z-­scores for NDI and ODI, and 
M-­distance are displayed in Figures 2 and 3. To evaluate for 
differences in z-­scores for NDI and ODI, and M-­distance 
across the four groups (i.e., controls, left TLE, right TLE, 
and bilateral TLE), we used the Kruskal–Wallis test. We 
then applied false discovery rate (FDR) correction sepa­
rately for NDI, ODI, and M-­distance (18 comparisons per 
measure). Regions with statistically significant group-­level 
differences (after FDR correction) are listed in Table S2. 
For NDI z-­score, significant differences were seen for 15 
of 18 regions after multiple comparisons correction. Less 
widespread differences were seen in ODI z-­score, with 
only four of 18 regions (right hippocampus, bilateral for­
nices, and left cingulum) showing statistically significant 
group-­level differences. For M-­distance, significant dif­
ferences were seen for 14 of 18 regions. When comparing 
regions based on the presence or absence of group-­level 
differences, only four of 18 (22%) regions showed consist­
ent group effects (i.e., limbic regions with similar group-­
level differences across NDI, ODI, and M-­distance). This 
indicates that a multivariate measure accounting for the 
unique contributions of NDI and ODI contributes unique 
information compared to either measure alone.
3.3  |  Diagnostic performance of LI in 
clinical lateralization of TLE
We next assessed the diagnostic performance of the LI of 
the M-­distance in clinical lateralization of TLE. The results 
for LI are shown in Table 2. The diagnostic performance 
for individual ROIs was highest for the hippocampus NDI 
univariate z-­score (area under the curve [AUC] = .87, 95% 
confidence interval [CI] = .62–.99) in all unilateral TLE 
participants. The diagnostic performance of the summary 
score (sum of individual ROIs) was highest for the M-­
distance (AUC = .95, 95% CI = .77–1) in MRI nonlesional 
unilateral TLE participants.
3.4  |  Burden of limbic microstructural 
abnormalities are associated with 
neuropsychological deficits and surgical 
outcomes
To understand how limbic microstructural abnormalities 
associate with neuropsychological deficits and surgical 
outcome, we calculated the sum of the M-­distance for the 
nine mesial temporal ROIs in each hemisphere.
Among participants with left hemispheric neuro­
psychological deficits, the summary score for the left 
hemisphere was similar (median = 34.6, interquartile 
range [IQR] = 25.2–41.4) to the right hemisphere (me­
dian = 27.8, IQR = 21.6–44.2, p = .3). Among participants

4  |  DISCUSSION
In this study, we demonstrate the unique effects of neu­
rite density and neurite coherence in limbic regions in 
TLE. When accounting for both neurite density and ori­
entation with multivariate statistics (i.e., M-­distance), we 
show unique patterns of abnormalities not captured by 
either measure alone. The M-­distance achieved high di­
agnostic accuracy in clinical lateralization of TLE, with 
AUC = .95 (95% CI = .77–1) for the summary score in MRI 
nonlesional unilateral TLE participants. Among patients 
who underwent ablative or resective surgery, summary 
scores were lower among those who were seizure-­free at

in the hemisphere ipsilateral to surgery (with a nonsignifi­
cant trend in the contralateral hemisphere). We found that 
participants with unilateral TLE who were not seizure-­free 
at 12-­months postsurgery had similar summary scores to 
those with bilateral TLE. Using elastic net regression with 
nested cross-­validation, we found that a model including 
ipsilateral and contralateral summary scores had high ac­
curacy in predicting 12-­month surgical outcome. Finally, 
we provide patient-­level data to supplement our quantita­
tive analysis and suggest potential explanations why pre­
dictions may fail. Taken together, these findings indicate 
that mapping limbic microstructural abnormalities in TLE 
using normative modeling and multivariate statistics repre­
sents a tool that warrants further study as a precision medi­
cine tool in the presurgical evaluation of drug-­resistant 
TLE, especially when used alongside clinical data.
In this study, we found microstructural abnormalities in 
both limbic gray and white matter. In prior work, Winston 
et  al.12 showed that in TLE NDI is reduced in the mesial 
and basal temporal cortex ipsilateral to seizure onset, with 
more widespread reduction in NDI in the subcortical white 
matter. Giachetti et al.14 investigated hippocampal NODDI 
abnormalities in a cohort of patients with TLE. They found 
significant abnormalities in hippocampal NDI, ODI, and free 
water. The latter finding underscores the importance of cor­
rection for CSF partial volume effects and potential for this to 
bias findings from prior studies in TLE focused on the hippo­
campus and other structures abutting the ventricles (e.g., for­
nix).15 In the current study, our goal was to mitigate bias from 
CSF partial volume effects and focus on regional (limbic) ab­
normalities using multivariate statistics that simultaneously 
consider factors shown in prior studies to be abnormal in 
TLE, namely neurite density and neurite coherence.
An additional strength of this study is that it aggregates 
the abnormalities in microstructure across different regions 
in the limbic system described in prior studies12,14 into a 
single composite score based on normative data. Such 
normative modeling-­based measures have the potential to 
serve as precision MRI biomarkers in epilepsy.17 In prior 
work by our group, we showed the utility of summary 
scores representing the aggregate burden of brain imaging 
abnormalities in mapping multiple epilepsy phenotypes.

For example, one study24 showed that summary scores 
representing the burden of abnormalities in morphomet­
ric features from structural MRI and white matter mi­
crostructure from dMRI were associated with incident 
(future) diagnosis of late onset epilepsy in participants in 
the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study. Two other 
studies showed that the aggregate burden of structural 
connectivity abnormalities inferred from diffusion tractog­
raphy was associated with seizure freedom after temporal 
lobectomy29 as well as seizure semiology (i.e., presence of 
focal to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures) in TLE.30 Our find­
ings are also in agreement with another study that utilized 
graph theoretical measures of network integration and seg­
regation derived from resting state functional MRI. The au­
thors applied dimensionality reduction to multiple graph 
theoretical measures to derive a summary score describing 
a participant's location along an “integration–segregation 
axis.” They showed that unilateral TLE participants who 
were not seizure-­free were more similar to those with bilat­
eral TLE than those with unilateral TLE who were seizure-­
free postsurgery.31 A somewhat surprising finding is that 
the diagnostic accuracy of the lateralization index of the M-­
distance in clinical lateralization of TLE was higher in non­
lesional patients (as opposed to the entire cohort of both 
lesional and nonlesional subjects). This could be explained 
by nonspecific pathology in the contralateral hemisphere 
or a disproportionate amount of bilateral pathology in the 
lesional group. Regardless, the greatest clinical utility of 
such a tool would be in the nonlesional patient, so higher 
accuracy in this group is reassuring.
To our knowledge, prior studies have not evaluated piri­
form cortex microstructure in human epilepsy in vivo. The 
piriform cortex is similar to the hippocampus in that it has 
three-­layered cortex, has extensive recurrent projections, 
is sensitive to excitotoxic injury, and is implicated in epi­
leptogenesis.4 Despite these similarities, the piriform cor­
tex has received much less attention in epilepsy research, 
likely in part related to the lack of automatic segmentation 
algorithms. In this work, we used publicly available human 
piriform cortex atlases21 and multiatlas segmentation tech­
niques22 to map piriform cortex.32 We found that patients 
with TLE had lower NDI than controls in bilateral piriform 
cortices, but there was no difference between TLE and con­
trols for piriform ODI. Differences in M-­distance between 
TLE patients and controls were seen in right but not left 
piriform cortex. The piriform cortex had only modest value 
in clinical lateralization of TLE, with an AUC of .58 (and 
.76 for nonlesional patients) for M-­distance.
Given that this study involves in vivo imaging, we can 
only speculate as to the neuropathologic correlates of NDI, 
ODI, and multivariate abnormalities in NDI and ODI. 
Furthermore, we studied white matter and gray matter re­
gions, the latter of which have not been comprehensively 
validated with histopathology. There is one small study that 
assessed the correspondence between NODDI measures and 
quantitative metrics from spinal cord histology in multiple 
sclerosis patients and controls, suggesting that both white 
and gray matter NODDI measures recapitulate histopatho­
logic measures of neurite orientation dispersion.33 The main 
histopathological features of hippocampal sclerosis include 
pyramidal cell loss and gliosis. There is a wide range of sever­
ity of these features across patients as well as variable subfield 
involvement.34 NDI may serve as a readout of pyramidal cell 
loss and ODI as a readout of selective fiber reorganization.14 
A recent study also suggested that ODI correlated with glia 
density,35 and gliosis is a universal neuropathologic feature 
in epilepsy surgical specimens.36 Future studies using mul­
tivariate scores derived from diffusion tensor imaging (e.g., 
from fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity) may also 
be informative. Acquisition of multishell dMRI suitable for 
NODDI fitting requires longer scan times, whereas diffusion 
tensor imaging utilizes single shell data, which is more feasi­
ble in a clinical setting. Additional limitations include sample 
size and cohort heterogeneity. To underscore the heterogene­
ity, less than half of patients underwent potentially curative 
surgery, whereas others underwent either palliative surgery 
or neuomodulation. The cohort also included numerous dif­
ferent structural etiologies (e.g., hippocampal sclerosis, focal 
cortical dysplasia), mirroring clinical practice. We attempted 
to control for the effects of structural lesions by separately 
analyzing nonlesional TLE patients; however, this reduced 
the overall sample size. Nonetheless, results were robust to 
the inherent reduction in sample size when analyzing this 
subgroup. Future studies with larger sample sizes are needed 
to determine the value of limbic microstructural abnormal­
ities as a tool to be used alongside clinical data in selecting 
the most appropriate surgical therapy and surgical outcome 
prediction. Another limitation is that the multivariate score 
only considers abnormalities among the nine a priori chosen 
regions per hemisphere. Using patient-­level data, we sug­
gest several reasons why such a measure may fail to accu­
rately predict outcome. We thus posit that the use of such 
a tool should be evaluated in future studies as a potential 
biomarker used alongside a typical multimodal presurgical 
evaluation in patients with TLE. Future studies should eval­
uate whether the burden of limbic abnormalities may aide 
in the selection of patients for smaller ablative procedures 
versus larger resective surgeries or whether a patient should 
undergo neuromodulation versus potentially curative sur­
gery. Again, these future studies would benefit from larger 
sample sizes that would permit the use of an independent 
hold-­out set for model testing.
This study offers unique insights on abnormalities in 
neurite density and neurite coherence in the limbic sys­
tem in TLE. Multivariate abnormalities accounting for the 
unique contributions from neurite density and orientation

Abstract: Objective: Widespread structural pathology in the limbic system is a hallmark of temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). In this work, we sought to describe a comprehen­ sive readout of limbic abnormalities in TLE using neurite orientation distribution and density imaging (NODDI). Methods: This is a retrospective study of patients with drug-­resistant TLE and healthy controls who underwent research magnetic resonance imaging. We es­ timated the degree of deviation of the NODDI parameters neurite density index (NDI) and orientation dispersion index (ODI) from healthy controls in limbic regions in the form of univariate z-­scores. We calculated a multivariate deviation score combining both NDI and ODI (Mahalanobis distance). A summary score representing the overall level of deviation across limbic regions was then com­ puted using the sum of regional deviation scores. We next assessed the diagnostic performance of summary scores in lateralizing TLE as well as associations with neuropsychological deficits and 12-­month surgical outcome. Results: The Mahalanobis distance revealed unique patterns of abnormalities between TLE participants (n = 74) and controls (n = 42), with only four of 18 (22%) areas displaying overlapping univariate and multivariate deviations. The multivariate summary score achieved the highest diagnostic accuracy in clinical lateralization of nonlesional TLE (area under the curve [AUC] = .95, 95% confi­ dence interval [CI] = .77–1). Among surgical patients (n = 30), summary scores corresponding to the hemisphere ipsilateral and contralateral to surgery were predictive of seizure freedom at 12 months (AUC = .84, 95% CI = .76–.93). Significance: We demonstrate unique patterns of abnormalities in neurite den­ sity and coherence in limbic microstructure in TLE.
